headline: 322 days at sea. The Lincoln is home.
summary: The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday, 322 days after it left for the Middle East. The deployment was meant to end in the summer. Food ran tight on board and the crew's mental health wore down. On Wednesday Pete Hegseth gave the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest award a unit can get.

cover_question.q: How long were they on the boat?

cover_answer: 322 days. They docked in San Diego on Thursday.
table_question: Can a medal make up for being kept away too long?

5-7.script: A huge Navy ship called the Lincoln came home to San Diego today. Its sailors were gone 322 days, longer than a whole school year, and the ship was meant to be back by summer. Food ran short and people got worn out. Now it is tied up at the dock, and the crew got the top prize a ship can get.
5-7.why: A school year is the longest stretch they can picture. The dock is the ending.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script measures 322 days against the one long stretch they know, a school year, and ends at the dock. The food running short is the vivid feature they will keep, so it comes with the prize. Expect "did they miss Christmas?" Yes. 322 days back is last November.

8-12.script: The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday after 322 days away. The Navy planned to have it home by summer and kept it out. Food ran tight and mental health wore down: a road trip where the driver keeps saying one more hour. On Wednesday Hegseth gave the crew the top award.
8-12.why: Planned, extended, ran short, home. The road trip is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults keep their word, so the script hands them the chain: a summer end date, an extension, food running low, a dock on Thursday. The road trip with one more hour is a mechanism they have sat through. Expect "why didn't they just come home?" A warship leaves when it is told.

13-17.script: Is a medal fair pay for 322 days away? The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday, past the homecoming its crew expected, after food ran tight and mental health wore down. The day before, Hegseth gave them the top unit award. Second: who decides a ship stays out?
13-17.why: The award is real. So was the cost.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the crew earned the highest unit award, and the same crew was kept out past its date with the food running low. The script puts the medal next to the cost and asks whether one pays for the other. Expect "would you have stayed?" Sailors don't get the choice. Say whether you'd want one.

5-7.q: How long were they on the boat?
5-7.a: 322 days, longer than a school year. They came home to San Diego on Thursday.

8-12.q: Why did it take so long?
8-12.a: It was meant to end in summer and got extended. Food ran tight.
The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest a unit can get.

13-17.q: Is a medal fair pay for 322 days away?
13-17.a: They got the top award. The Hill reports tight food and worn-down crews.

13-17.q: Who decides a ship stays out?
13-17.a: The Navy and the Pentagon. The crew doesn't vote.
